## Understanding the problem

Same points/ranking computation as before, plus a tier assignment: split teams into Tier 1 (top ~33%), Tier 2 (next ~33%), Tier 3 (bottom ~34%) by points, with ties at a tier boundary placed in the HIGHER tier.

With n = 10: Tier 1 gets ceil(0.33·10) = 4 teams, Tier 2 the next 4, Tier 3 the last 2 — matching the example (Sheffield United…Chelsea in Tier 1; Burnley…Luton Town in Tier 2; Liverpool, Aston Villa in Tier 3).

Elegant trick: tiers are fully determined by cutoff POINT VALUES, not positions. Take the points of the team at row-number ceil(0.33n) (call p1) and at ceil(0.66n) (call p2). Then points ≥ p1 ⇒ Tier 1, points ≥ p2 ⇒ Tier 2, else Tier 3. Because tied teams share the same points, they automatically fall in the same (higher) tier — the tie rule is handled for free.
k: Rank with RANK() (gaps on ties) for position; NTILE would break the tie-at-boundary rule.
Tier cutoffs are point values at row numbers ceil(0.33n) and ceil(0.66n) of the points-descending order.
Comparing points against cutoff values places boundary ties in the higher tier automatically.

a.i: Number teams 1..n by points DESC (team_name tiebreak for determinism), extract the points at the two boundary row numbers, then classify every team by comparing its points to those cutoffs. Position comes from RANK().
s: CTE r: points = wins*3+draws, rn = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, team_name), n = COUNT(*) OVER ().
CTE c: p1 = points at rn = CEIL(0.33·n), p2 = points at rn = CEIL(0.66·n).
Final select: RANK() for position, CASE on points vs p1/p2 for tier; ORDER BY points DESC, team_name.

c.python:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT team_name, wins * 3 + draws AS points,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY wins * 3 + draws DESC, team_name) AS rn,
         COUNT(*) OVER () AS n
  FROM TeamStats
),
c AS (
  SELECT MAX(CASE WHEN rn = CEIL(n * 0.33) THEN points END) AS p1,
         MAX(CASE WHEN rn = CEIL(n * 0.66) THEN points END) AS p2
  FROM r
)
SELECT r.team_name, r.points,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY r.points DESC) AS position,
       CASE WHEN r.points >= c.p1 THEN 'Tier 1'
            WHEN r.points >= c.p2 THEN 'Tier 2'
            ELSE 'Tier 3' END AS tier
FROM r, c
ORDER BY r.points DESC, r.team_name ASC;

a.i: NTILE(3) splits rows into three near-equal buckets by order, but assigns boundary ties arbitrarily (by the tiebreak), violating the higher-tier rule. You can post-correct: any team whose points equal the points of the first team of the NEXT tier is promoted. More convoluted than Approach 1, shown mainly to illustrate why NTILE alone fails.
s: tier_raw = NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY points DESC, team_name).
Find the minimum points within each raw tier; promote teams whose points equal the next tier's maximum-points boundary.
Map raw tiers 1/2/3 to labels after promotion.

c.python:
WITH r AS (
  SELECT team_name, wins * 3 + draws AS points,
         NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY wins * 3 + draws DESC, team_name) AS tk,
         MIN(wins * 3 + draws) OVER (PARTITION BY NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY wins * 3 + draws DESC, team_name)) AS mn
  FROM TeamStats
)
SELECT team_name, points,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY points DESC) AS position,
       CASE
         WHEN tk = 1 OR (tk = 2 AND points = (SELECT MAX(mn) FROM r WHERE tk = 2)) THEN 'Tier 1'
         WHEN tk = 2 OR (tk = 3 AND points = (SELECT MAX(mn) FROM r WHERE tk = 3)) THEN 'Tier 2'
         ELSE 'Tier 3'
       END AS tier
FROM r
ORDER BY points DESC, team_name ASC;

## Wrap-up

Approach 1 is cleaner and provably matches the tie rule; prefer it. Pitfalls: using NTILE blindly (ties straddle tiers), using FLOOR instead of CEIL for the 33% cutoff (off-by-one team), and forgetting RANK() gaps in position. Follow-up: parameterize the number of tiers, or tier by goal difference as a secondary criterion.
